content: The fortified cereal mix is specifically designed for infants and young children (IYC). For each of the three items analyzed, the nutrient profile is determined solely by the nutrient content of the selected item. Non-target nutrients are also considered in the analysis. The term MNP refers to multiple micronutrient powder, SCP stands for Super Cereal Plus, SQ-LNS represents small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements, and SSB indicates sugar-sweetened beverages. Nutrient values are generally expressed per 100 grams, except for MNP and SQ-LNS, where specific adjustments are made. For grains, nutrient values are based on raw or dry forms, with adjustments applied for retention after cooking methods such as boiling or steaming maize flour and rice. For iron content, the value for ferrous fumarate was used because the specifications for MNP and SQ-LNS indicate a mix of iron forms, with the majority being ferrous iron. This approach was also applied to SCP to ensure a more accurate comparison. The nutrient profiles for Optifood modeling focus on target vitamins and choline. These include vitamin A (measured in micrograms of retinol equivalents), thiamin, riboflavin, vitamin B6, folate (measured in micrograms of dietary folate equivalents), choline, and vitamin B12. Non-target nutrients, such as niacin and fatty acids like alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) and linoleic acid (LA), are also included. Niacin equivalents (NE) were calculated as the sum of niacin in milligrams and tryptophan divided by 60. Missing tryptophan data for approximately 30% of items was assessed, and it was determined that these gaps did not bias the mean niacin equivalent values. For fatty acids, nutrient values for ALA and LA were available for fewer than one-quarter of food items. When specific values were unavailable, undifferentiated 18:3 and 18:2 fatty acid values were used as substitutes. Grain nutrient values were adjusted for retention after cooking, as described earlier. The selection of parameters for Optifood modeling was based primarily on the analysis of available datasets, supplemented with additional sources when necessary. Published papers and reports were often too heterogeneous in their use of food groups and subgroups to be directly comparable. However, for certain items or subgroups, prevalence of consumption and median gram amounts were considered relevant for parameter selection. Optifood models food patterns on a weekly basis, using a mix of daily and weekly parameters. These include median grams per day at the food subgroup level (referred to as daily servings), the maximum number of days per week a food subgroup can be consumed, and the maximum number of daily servings per week at the broad food group level. Methodological choices aimed to allow for generous yet realistic amounts of nutrient-dense food subgroups. For infants aged 9 months, data on food consumption guided parameter selection. However, due to the lack of globally representative data, judgment was also employed in setting final parameters. For example, food subgroup-level data from datasets with fewer than 20 consumers were excluded to address outliers. Median daily servings were often based on the average of the two highest country medians, with adjustments made for high outliers. For specific food items like starchy roots, tubers, and plantains, median daily intakes ranged from 9 to 60 grams across datasets from eight countries. The average of the two highest medians (~53 grams in Mexico and ~60 grams in Kenya) was used to set the parameter at 60 grams per day. Similarly, for pork, median daily intakes ranged from 15 to 27 grams across seven countries, with the top two medians averaging 26 grams. However, data from regions like East and Southeast Asia, where pork consumption is higher, were not represented. For Vietnam, a daily serving size of 35 grams was used based on local analysis. Breastfed infants posed unique challenges. High milk intakes observed in some countries (over 200 grams) could displace breastfeeding. To address this, milk intake parameters were adjusted to reflect realistic consumption patterns while still promoting nutrient density in complementary foods. The maximum number of days per week a food subgroup can be consumed was estimated based on the percentage of children consuming the subgroup on recall days, following methods described in previous research. This estimation assumes independence of daily consumption and a stationary probability across the week. The resulting maximum days per week were determined using a binomial distribution model. For breakfast cereals, the same maximum frequency was applied to both whole-grain and refined-grain cereals to avoid bias toward refined grains, which are empirically consumed in larger quantities. Sensitivity analyses were also conducted, allowing all food subgroups a maximum of seven daily servings per week. At the broad food group level, Optifood constraints are expressed in terms of the number of daily servings allowed across all subgroups within the group. Weekly frequencies were estimated by counting the number of subgroups consumed within each main food group and multiplying by seven. Percentiles of these weekly frequencies were calculated, and the 90th percentile values were used to set maximum constraints. In developing food patterns to approximate real-world situations, data from countries like Bangladesh, Malawi, and Mexico were used. These patterns were characterized by the percentage of energy from food groups and subgroups, which were then translated into grams per subgroup. Rescaling was necessary to estimate grams per subgroup due to observed energy intake variations.
